messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode of care described below. A three-character category is one capital letter followed by exactly two digits, for example J44.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient: 66-year-old woman

Hospital Course: The patient presented with bilateral cramping thigh pain for three days. She had a past medical history of coronary artery disease, heart failure, high cholesterol, high blood pressure, and diabetes. She was previously hospitalized for a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment: The patient received aggressive intravenous hydration and her simvastatin and ticagrelor medications were discontinued. Her symptoms resolved and laboratory tests showed improvement. She was started on a new medication, clopidogrel, and was prescribed rosuvastatin during a follow-up clinic visit.

Follow-up: The patient has remained without complications on follow-up visits and laboratory tests.

Conclusion: The patient was discharged in stable condition with appropriate medications and follow-up care.

Reply with the three characters only.

text:
The picture suggests statin-induced rhabdomyolysis, possibly with an interaction between simvastatin and ticagrelor, which raises simvastatin levels. Treatment was aggressive IV hydration, simvastatin was stopped, and laboratory tests improved, which fits rhabdomyolysis with raised CK.

In ICD-10-AM, rhabdomyolysis is coded M62.8 (Other specified disorders of muscle), and M62.82 is the specific code in ICD-10-CM. The drug-induced form could also be coded as myopathy, G72.0 (drug-induced myopathy). The ICD-10-AM index lists "Rhabdomyolysis (idiopathic)" under M62.8, and "Myopathy, drug-induced" under G72.0. With bilateral thigh cramping pain, hydration, and improving labs, rhabdomyolysis is the more likely diagnosis, so I chose M62.

M62
